segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: After the pandemic, horror became the safest bet at the box office. From Smile and Barbarian to The Substance and Sinners, the genre broke out of its niche, won over the Oscars and spread around the world.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: The 2010s ended with horror rehabilitated, and the 2020s began with it in the lead. When The Invisible Man (2020) hit theaters in late February 2020, no one imagined that, weeks later, cinemas around the world would close their doors because of the pandemic. When they reopened, the genre showed an advantage blockbusters lacked: cheap films with loyal audiences that depend neither on expensive stars nor on effects that eat up hundreds of millions of dollars. In 2021, according to the website The Numbers, horror accounted for 12.9% of tickets sold in the United States, the highest share ever recorded for the genre up to that point (surpassed only in 2025). What looked like a side effect of an empty market became the rule: in the years that followed, horror established itself as Hollywood's most reliable bet and achieved a prestige it had rarely enjoyed.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: The pandemic also taught studios to send horror straight to streaming, and it was test screenings that changed their minds. Smile (2022), Parker Finn's feature debut, had been made for Paramount+; after very positive test screenings, Paramount took it to theaters in September 2022. It cost US$ 17 million and earned US$ 217 million, helped by a simple and unsettling marketing stunt: actors smiling fixedly behind home plate during televised baseball games. Around the same time, Barbarian (2022) escaped being sent straight to Hulu. Written and directed by Zach Cregger, a comedian from the troupe The Whitest Kids U' Know, the film begins as a thriller about a double-booked rental house and changes course several times. Made on a US$ 4.5 million budget, it grossed US$ 46 million worldwide.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: If Blumhouse was horror's assembly line, A24 became its designer label. The distributor of The Witch and Hereditary (2018) used the pandemic for an experiment: Ti West shot two features back to back, in secret, in New Zealand, with the same star, Mia Goth. In X (2022), a tribute to 1970s slashers about a crew shooting an adult film on a Texas farm, Goth plays both young Maxine and the elderly Pearl. Months later, Pearl (2022) told the origin story of the murderous old woman in the saturated colors of old musicals, and the trilogy wrapped up with MaXXXine (2024). In 2023, the distributor went to YouTube to find the Australian brothers Danny and Michael Philippou, whose Talk to Me (2023) became A24's highest-grossing horror film up to that point — a story told in the next chapter.

tracks.title: Learn more: A24: the brand that became a genre

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: Learn more: A24: the brand that became a genre.
segments.text: Learn more: A24: the brand that became a genre.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: Founded in New York in August 2012 by Daniel Katz, David Fenkel and John Hodges, A24 did something rare in the film business: it turned a distributor's logo into a promise of style. For many viewers, “an A24 movie” became almost a subgenre, with a slow pace, an oppressive atmosphere, a static camera and endings that don't explain everything. The company cultivated that identity with auteur-style posters, merchandise for fans and messaging that treats every release as a cinephile event. Its credibility also came from awards: in 2023, Everything Everywhere All at Once (2022) gave the distributor its second Best Picture Oscar, after Moonlight in 2017. In horror, that prestige helped popularize the label elevated horror, used by the American press to set “auteur” films apart from “ordinary” horror. Many genre critics reject the term: in 2018, Jacob Knight wrote in SlashFilm that the distinction ignores classics like The Exorcist and The Texas Chain Saw Massacre, which were already art and entertainment at the same time. The 2020s proved him right: in 2026, the highest-grossing film in A24's history was Backrooms (2026), an adaptation of a YouTube web series that passed US$ 400 million worldwide — a story told in another chapter.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: A24's direct competitor on this turf is Neon, the distributor that made its name with Palme d'Or winners such as Parasite and Titane (2021). Its biggest ace in the genre was Longlegs (2024), by Osgood Perkins, son of Anthony Perkins, the Norman Bates of Psycho. The release campaign became a case study: teasers just a few seconds long, coded messages, an encrypted ad in the Seattle Times that evoked the Zodiac Killer, billboards with a phone number that played sinister recordings, and not a single clear image of the villain played by Nicolas Cage. The mystery worked as bait. In July 2024, the film opened with US$ 22.4 million in the United States, the biggest opening in Neon's history, and finished with US$ 128 million worldwide, having cost less than US$ 10 million.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: No film sums up the new wave better than The Substance (2024), by French director Coralie Fargeat. In the story, a fading TV star, fired on her 50th birthday, injects a substance that generates a younger version of herself, on one condition: the two must switch places every seven days. The rest is an escalation of blood, prosthetics and satire about Hollywood's obsession with youth. Awarded for its screenplay at Cannes in 2024, the film was dropped by Universal in a dispute over final cut, ended up being distributed by MUBI and became the company's biggest box-office hit. It earned five Oscar nominations, including Best Picture, Director and Actress, and won for Makeup and Hairstyling. For Demi Moore, it was a career turnaround: a Golden Globe, a Screen Actors Guild Award and the first Oscar nomination of her life.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: Prestige horror also looked back. Robert Eggers, who had made his debut with The Witch, realized a project he had been chasing since his teens: remaking Nosferatu, eine Symphonie des Grauens (Nosferatu, 1922), F. W. Murnau's expressionist classic. His Nosferatu (2024) traded the vampire's cut-out silhouette for a decomposing count, nearly unrecognizable under Bill Skarsgård's makeup, and placed at its center Lily-Rose Depp's Ellen, a young woman tormented since childhood by a presence that desires her. Released in the United States on Christmas 2024, it cost US$ 50 million and grossed US$ 182 million, the biggest box office of Eggers's career. It received four Oscar nominations, for Cinematography, Costume Design, Production Design and Makeup, but won none: it lost the Makeup award, of all things, to The Substance.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: At the other end, popular horror had its own boom. Jason Blum's Blumhouse finalized its merger with James Wan's Atomic Monster in January 2024, and had its biggest hit with a film critics loathed: Five Nights at Freddy's (2023), an adaptation of an indie video game. Even though it was released simultaneously on the Peacock streaming service, it grossed US$ 297 million worldwide, Blumhouse's highest-grossing film up to that point, propelled by fans who had grown up watching the game on YouTube. Damien Leone, meanwhile, financed part of Terrifier 2 (2022) through online crowdfunding: the film cost US$ 250,000, earned US$ 15.8 million and became notorious for reports of viewers getting sick during screenings. In October 2024, Terrifier 3 opened at No. 1 in the United States and, with US$ 90 million, became the highest-grossing unrated film in history.

tracks.title: Learn more: The body as horror: the body horror revival

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: Learn more: The body as horror: the body horror revival.
segments.text: Learn more: The body as horror: the body horror revival.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: Body horror, the horror born of the body's own transformations, mutilations and revolts, has a patron saint: David Cronenberg, who turned the genre into a study of desire, technology and disease in films like The Fly (1986), winner of the Oscar for Makeup. In the 2020s, this kind of cinema left the midnight screenings and moved to the center of the festivals. In 2021, Julia Ducournau won the Palme d'Or for Titane, the story of a killer who becomes pregnant after an encounter with a car; she was only the second woman to win the prize, after Jane Campion in 1993. The following year, Cronenberg himself returned to Cannes with Crimes of the Future (2022). The Substance carried the trend to the Oscars and, in 2026, the Makeup category also nominated the Norwegian Den stygge stesøsteren (The Ugly Stepsister, 2025), a gory retelling of Cinderella told from the side of the stepsister who mutilates her own body to fit the slipper. The thread connecting these films is clear: the body became the stage on which the anxieties of the era play out, from aging and beauty standards to motherhood and gender identity.

segments.original: Between these two poles, Jordan Peele kept making films that defy pigeonholing. After Get Out and Us, he released Nope (2022), a blend of western, science fiction and monster movie about a brother and sister who train horses for Hollywood productions and try to photograph something hiding in the clouds above the family ranch. Shot partly with IMAX cameras, the film is also a reflection on spectacle: on who profits from the image and who gets devoured by it. It grossed US$ 171 million worldwide. It did not have the impact of Get Out, but it reinforced what Peele had shown in the previous decade: horror could be the space for Black filmmakers to tell the American story on their own terms. Three years later, that idea would reach its peak.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: That peak goes by the name of Sinners (2025). Written and directed by Ryan Coogler, the film is set in 1932 Mississippi: twins Smoke and Stack, both played by Michael B. Jordan, return to their hometown to open a blues joint and, on opening night, are visited by vampires. Coogler uses the myth to talk about cultural heritage, the appropriation of Black music and the violence of the segregated South. With a budget of US$ 90 million to US$ 100 million, the film grossed US$ 370 million worldwide, an exceedingly rare result for an original story. At the 2026 Oscars, it received 16 nominations, an all-time record that surpassed the 14 earned by All About Eve, Titanic and La La Land. It won four: Actor for Jordan, Original Screenplay for Coogler, Original Score for Ludwig Göransson and Cinematography for Autumn Durald Arkapaw, the first woman to win in that category. Best Picture went to One Battle After Another.

segments.original: Sinners did not come alone: 2025 was Warner Bros.'s year in the genre. The Conjuring: Last Rites (2025) closed out the Warrens' saga with US$ 499 million, the highest gross in the series, and Zach Cregger, of Barbarian, returned with Weapons (2025). Its premise is a fairy-tale mystery: at 2:17 one morning, seventeen children from the same class run out of their homes and vanish into the dark, and only one student is left behind. Told in chapters, each from a different character's point of view, the film mixes horror, acid humor and a tension many read as an allegory for the collective traumas of American towns. It cost US$ 38 million and reached US$ 270 million worldwide. The scene-stealer was veteran Amy Madigan as Aunt Gladys: forty years after her only previous nomination, she won the Oscar for Best Supporting Actress in March 2026.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: While Hollywood was discovering the genre's prestige, the rest of the world was proving its commercial muscle. In South Korea, Exhuma (2024), by Jang Jae-hyun, follows a shaman, her apprentice, a mortician and a geomancer hired to move a cursed grave and, beneath the scares, probes the wounds of the Japanese occupation. Released in February 2024, it drew 11.9 million moviegoers and was the country's first occult film to pass 10 million admissions. In Indonesia, the phenomenon is even bigger: in 2024, about 60% of the 258 local films released were horror, and the genre sold 54.6 million tickets. The most respected name in this wave is Joko Anwar, whose Pengabdi Setan 2: Communion (Satan's Slaves 2: Communion, 2022) was the first Indonesian film released in IMAX and drew 6.3 million people to theaters.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: Some of the decade's most frightening films came from Latin America. Argentina's Cuando acecha la maldad (When Evil Lurks, 2023), by Demián Rugna, about a demonic possession spreading through the countryside, became in 2023 the first Latin American film to win Best Picture at the Sitges Film Festival. In Mexico, Michelle Garza Cervera made her debut with Huesera: The Bone Woman (2023), a body horror film about a mother-to-be haunted by a figure of twisted bones, which won awards at Tribeca. And Guillermo del Toro finally made his Frankenstein (2025), which took home three Oscars in 2026; added to the four for Sinners and Amy Madigan's, that made eight statuettes for monster stories in a single night. From Australia, besides Talk to Me, came Late Night with the Devil (2024), a fake 1977 talk show that ends in tragedy. Six years after theaters went dark, horror no longer asks permission: it packs theaters, wins awards and keeps turning each era's fears into a collective experience in the dark.
